title: Lehman's laws, seen from inside a loan origination platform
body: Lehman wrote his laws about large systems in the 1970s, and I still meet them every sprint. Our consumer vehicle loan origination platform at Winjit is a set of .NET microservices that handle applications, document checks and credit decisions.

Continuing change shows up first. Every new lender rule, scorecard or document type means the system has to change, or it becomes less useful to the people who rely on it. We never reach a finished state.

Increasing complexity is the law you can feel. Each rule we add makes the next one harder unless we spend time on refactoring. We now reserve part of each sprint for that work, and we treat it as planned work, not as a favour.
The lesson I am taking into the MSc: evolution is the normal state of real software. The design question is how to make change cheap, safe and visible.

title: Week one in Limerick: from writing code to studying how code changes
body: After more than six years at Winjit in Nashik, I have started the MSc in Software Engineering at the University of Limerick.

The Software Evolution module is the one I was most curious about. In industry we talk about legacy code, technical debt and refactoring every day, but we rarely use a shared vocabulary for them. This module gives me that vocabulary.

This portfolio is part of that work. Version 1 is the first release, and the Readme page records every change as a typed maintenance activity, so the site itself becomes an example of software evolution.

title: Adding a new bank to an OCR pipeline is an adaptive change
body: Our bank statement extractor reads PDF statements from South African banks and turns them into structured transactions. Each bank lays its statement out differently, so each one needs its own positional extractor, with Google Gemini as a fallback when the layout is unclear.

When we added Nedbank and Capitec, no requirement changed for users. The environment changed: new input formats arrived. In the maintenance taxonomy (Lientz and Swanson, later ISO/IEC 14764) that is adaptive maintenance.

The bug fixes that followed were corrective: sign errors, misread digits, batches cut short and a race condition in parallel processing. Adding validation and de-duplication was preventive work, because it stops the next class of errors before users see them.
Labelling each change this way made our sprint reviews clearer. It also showed us that most of our effort was not new features at all.
